 1                       MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES

 2 I.       INTRODUCTION

 3          Wiwynn’s core claim is simple. Wiwynn alleges that X owes it money for computer

 4 components that X never purchased, under a comprehensive contract that fully spells out X’s

 5 obligations. But since the contract does not say what Wiwynn wants it to say, Wiwynn tries to locate

 6 liability somewhere else. When two sophisticated companies enter into a fully integrated master

 7 agreement, however, blackletter law dictates that their relationship is governed by that written

 8 contract and that contract alone. None of Wiwynn’s amorphous allegations about extrinsic

 9 understandings and unstated agreements can change the parties’ written contract. Wiwynn fails to

10 state a claim because its causes of action contradict the clear terms of the parties’ agreement.

11 II.      ARGUMENT

17 is MPA Section 4.3.3, which says:

18                  Forecast. Forecast provided by [X] for [Wiwynn’s] standard
                    Components are non-binding. For non-standard Components (any
19                  Components that are customized per [X]’s request), [X] anticipates
                    providing [Wiwynn] with a six-month rolling forecast.
20

21

22
     six-month rolling forecasts for non-standard components by “negative implication” because the
23

24

25

19 and Product Exhibits constitute “the complete and exclusive understanding and agreement of the

20 parties,” and any change must be “in writing and signed by the parties.” MPA § 14.13.

19          B.      Promissory Estoppel

20                  1.      The integrated MPA bars Wiwynn’s promissory estoppel claim.

21          Wiwynn’s claims and the MPA concern the same subject matter: sales of servers by Wiwynn

22 to X. As noted above, the fully integrated MPA is the “complete and exclusive understanding” of

23 the parties as to that “subject matter.” MPA § 14.13. Thus, Wiwynn cannot state a claim for

24 promissory estoppel “because a valid contract, supported by consideration, governs the same subject

25 matter as the alleged promise.” KST Data, Inc. v. Northrop Grumman Sys. Corp., 2017 WL

 2 2d 1152, 1163 (C.D. Cal. 2009)); see also MTD at 14–15.

 3          For one thing, the “purpose of the doctrine of promissory estoppel is to permit a court of

 4 equity to excuse the absence of consideration for an otherwise enforceable promise.” JMP Sec. LLP

 5 v. Altair Nanotechnologies Inc., 880 F. Supp. 2d 1029, 1041 (N.D. Cal. 2012). But here, as in JMP,

 6 the “claim for promissory estoppel must fail because no party disputes that the promises at issue

 7 here were supported by consideration.” See id. Thus, “there is no need to provide a substitute for

 8 consideration,” making Wiwynn’s promissory estoppel claim “superfluous.” Leids v. Metlife Home

 9 Loans, 2009 WL 4894991, at *6 (C.D. Cal. Dec. 7, 2009).

10          The MPA also prevents Wiwynn from adequately alleging reliance. Wiwynn allegedly relied

11 on X’s promise by buying components that would be used to fill X’s potential Purchase Orders. The

12 MPA already required as much. See MTD at 14–15; MPA §§ 2.2; 2.4. Where the acts in reliance are

13 the same as those taken to fulfill preexisting duties under the contract, there can be no claim for

14 promissory estoppel. See Avidity Partners, LLC v. State of California, 221 Cal. App. 4th 1180, 1208–

15 09 (2013).5

16                  2.      Promissory estoppel cannot be pleaded in the alternative here.

17          Rather than engage with these arguments, Wiwynn claims it can plead promissory estoppel

18 and breach of contract as alternative theories. Resp. at 9–10. That is true in some cases, but not here.

19          “California courts have made clear that contract claims and promissory estoppel claims are

20 mutually exclusive and that courts can dismiss a cause of action for promissory estoppel even at the

21 pleading stage.” Distance Learning Co., Inc. v. Silly Monkey Studios, LLC, No. 16-CV-06943-SK,

22 2017 WL 9613958, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 14, 2017). When the scope or existence or validity of a

 7          “The covenant of good faith and fair dealing, implied by law in every contract, exists merely

 8 to prevent one contracting party from unfairly frustrating the other party’s right to receive the

 9 benefits of the agreement actually made.” Day v. GEICO Cas. Co., No. 21-CV-02103-BLF, 2022

10 WL 2135746, at *2 (N.D. Cal. June 14, 2022) (citing Guz v. Bechtel Nat. Inc., 24 Cal. 4th 317, 349

11 (2000)) (emphasis original). “But the implied covenant can neither substantively alter the terms of

12 the contract nor impose substantive duties or limits on the contracting parties beyond those

13 incorporated in the specific terms of their agreement.” Id. (cleaned up). Since the covenant

14 “functions as a supplement to the express contractual covenants,” the “precise nature and extent of

15 the duty imposed by the implied covenant depends upon the contours of the underlying contract.”

16 W. Am. Ins. v. Shaghal Ltd., No. CV2107751CJCJPRX, 2022 WL 17370532, at *3 (C.D. Cal. June

17 23, 2022) (quoting Thrifty Payless, Inc. v. The Americana at Brand, LLC, 218 Cal. App. 4th 1230,

18 1244 (2013) (emphasis original) (cleaned up)).

19          Adhering to these principles, courts routinely dismiss claims for breach of the covenant of

20 good faith and fair dealing that do not allege the “specific contractual provision” that was

21 frustrated.19 This gatekeeping is necessary: “To allow a party to plead a breach of contract claim

22 based on a violation of the covenant of good faith and fair dealing untethered from a specific

23 contractual provision would undermine the certainty a contract provides, especially in light of later

24 changed circumstances favorable to one party over the other.” Day, 2022 WL 2135746, at *2.

25

 1          Wiwynn’s claim for breach of the covenant of good faith and fair dealing does not refer to

 3                 2.      The implied covenant may not create new contract duties.

 4          Rather than identifying any frustrated provision of the parties’ contract, Wiwynn alleges that

 5 the MPA implied a covenant that X “would act in good faith and deal fairly,” “do nothing to interfere

 6 with Wiwynn’s interests and commitments,” and “give at least the same level of consideration to the

 7 interests of Wiwynn” as its own. FAC ¶ 49. The MPA, obviously, says nothing of the sort. The

 8 implied covenant “does not create a separate duty of fairness and reasonableness which can be

 9 independently breached.” See CAL. COM. CODE § 1304, cmt. 1. It only means that “a failure to

10 perform or enforce, in good faith, a specific duty or obligation under the contract, constitutes a

11 breach of that contract.” Id.

12          The Ninth Circuit rejected an argument like Wiwynn’s in Openshaw v. FedEx Ground

13 Package Sys., Inc., 576 F. App’x 685 (9th Cir. 2014). There, Openshaw claimed FedEx breached the

14 implied covenant by, for example, “not telling Openshaw in advance how many packages he would

15 have to deliver.” Id. at 688. However, their contract “explicitly obligated Openshaw to provide

16 trucks and drivers and to operate at a national standard.” Id. The Ninth Circuit thus ruled for FedEx,

17 as the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing could not be used “to impose a substantive

18 duty on FedEx to help Openshaw provide trucks and drivers or to meet delivery standards.” Id.

19 (emphasis original).

20          Wiwynn wants to shoehorn a brand-new contractual obligation on X to help Wiwynn fulfill

21 its own existing duty under the MPA to stock necessary components so that it can timely fill X’s

22 orders if and when they are made. Both Wiwynn and Openshaw would convert their counterparties’

23 rights to have their needs met (X’s demand for servers and FedEx’s for drivers) into a duty to make

24 it easier to meet them. That is beyond the implied covenant’s reach. Cf. Microsoft Corp. v. Hon Hai

25 Precision Indus. Co., No. 19-CV-01279-LHK, 2020 WL 836712, at *7–8 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 20, 2020)

26 (dismissing implied covenant claim that “would effectively write in a requirement that Microsoft
27 help Hon Hai perform its contract obligations”).

28          Wiwynn’s implied covenant claim is untethered from the law and thus warrants dismissal.

 3 foreclosed by the integrated MPA and the economic loss rule. They also give X no way to know

 4 which statements comprise the alleged fraud, falling well short of the heightened pleading standard.

 5                  1.     The integrated MPA defeats Wiwynn’s fraud claims.

 6          As shown above, the MPA is incompatible with the notion that X’s non-binding forecasts

 7 somehow became binding when X simply “approved” Wiwynn’s corresponding component lists.

 8          The MPA and Product Exhibits presume that Wiwynn alone bears costs incurred meeting its

 9 own obligations, MPA § 2.4; provide that forecasts are non-binding, id. § 4.3.3 and Product Exhibits

10 at 10; obligate Wiwynn to acquire sufficient inventory to meet forecasted orders, MPA § 6.2 and

11 Product Exhibits at 10; and place the pre-delivery risk of loss on Wiwynn subject to a single

12 (inapplicable) exception, MPA § 4.3.4. And the MPA is the parties’ fully integrated, “complete and

13 exclusive” contract, which cannot be changed without another signed agreement. MPA § 14.13.

14           The contradiction between Wiwynn’s fraud allegations and the MPA’s text ends the inquiry.

15 “California holds parties responsible for signing integrated contracts,” and thus “parol evidence

16 cannot be introduced to show fraud or misrepresentation if the parol evidence contradicts the

17 language of an integrated contract[.]” Brinderson–Newberg, 971 F.2d at 281. This is so where, as

18 here, “the false promise relates to the matter covered by the main agreement and contradicts or varies

19 the terms thereof.” Id. (citing Price v. Wells Fargo Bank, 213 Cal. App. 3d 465 (1989)).20

20                  2.     The economic loss rule bars Wiwynn’s fraud claims.

21          Wiwynn’s misrepresentation claims also run afoul of the economic loss rule. The

22 “fundamental rule in California is that no tort cause of action will lie where the breach of duty is
